name: Pay for performance: pros and cons
purpose: Why do organizations use PFP – and what does it cost them?

parts.label: Why organizations use it
points: Associated with higher performance (directing effort, motivating)
Attracts higher performers, encourages low performers to leave

apply: Weigh both columns with case evidence before recommending to keep, change or drop PFP

name: The uncertainty mechanism
origin: Sayre, Corgnet, Hernán González & Gächter (2026), MIT Sloan Management Review
purpose: Why does PFP harm employees? The problem is pay uncertainty, not PFP itself.

parts.label: Uncertainty
points: About what is rewarded and how much I will earn

parts.label: Insecurity
points: Financial insecurity, tunnel vision on earnings

parts.label: Overwork
points: Neglected recovery – people kept working even when pay became negligible

apply: Ask: how is PRP designed here, and what uncertainty does that design create?
pitfalls: Limits: lab experiments (5 studies, 1,400+ people, simple tasks, random token pay) – applying them to a sales team is an inference
example: Experiment: same average pay – a certain 12 tokens per correct answer vs an uncertain 1–23 tokens. The uncertain group worked longer and reported more stress.

name: Keep the benefits, reduce the costs: Clear, Smooth, Secure
purpose: How can organizations keep the benefits of PRP while reducing its costs?

parts.label: 1. Make the rules clear
points: Define goals/KPIs and bonus criteria in advance
Frequent feedback so employees know where they stand
→ less uncertainty about WHAT is rewarded

parts.label: 2. Smooth variable income
points: Team/company-level rather than purely individual outcomes

parts.label: 3. Reduce financial insecurity
points: Increase the proportion of base pay
→ less uncertainty about HOW MUCH employees earn

apply: Turn each fix into a concrete change for the case firm (two detailed recommendations are typical exam tasks)
pitfalls: Recommending “more base pay” without saying what happens to the performance focus
example: National Office Supplies: written bonus criteria for all offices (clear); replace the monthly top-seller prize and roll-over with annual results plus an office team share (smooth); turn Jeff's pot into a real London allowance (secure).

name: Collective pay for performance
origin: Nyberg et al. (2020) – meta-analysis of 106 studies
purpose: Does paying for collective outcomes (team PRP, gainsharing, profit sharing, stock options) work?

parts.label: Benefits
points: Positive overall relationship with collective outcomes (ρ = .11): financial, operational, behavioural
Common goals, knowledge sharing, cooperation and coordination – especially where work is interdependent

parts.label: Drawbacks
points: Trade-off between alignment and line of sight: the further the reward from what I influence, the weaker effort → performance → my reward
Teams optimizing at the expense of the wider organization

apply: Recommend collective PRP when work is interdependent; keep teams small or add individual recognition to protect line of sight
example: Scotland office (National Office Supplies): pot split equally – no uncertainty, but free-riding risk and little reason to stand out.

name: How to pay? Decisions to be made
purpose: Which design decisions make up a compensation system?
apply: Position the case's current package on each axis, then argue where it should move and why – always naming the trade-off
pitfalls: Answering only “how much” – the question is “what for” and “how”

name: Trade-offs in compensation design
purpose: Three criteria every reward system must balance.

parts.label: Direction
points: Does it promote the desired behaviour?

parts.label: Fairness
points: Is it perceived as fair (internal, external, procedural)?

parts.label: Workability
points: Can it be administered, explained, afforded?

apply: Assess the case's system on all three corners; a fix for one corner usually costs another (e.g. precise individual targets: direction ↑, workability ↓)
pitfalls: Analysing only direction (motivation) and forgetting fairness and workability

name: Herzberg's two-factor model
purpose: Why “rewards & compensation are different things”: pay can remove dissatisfaction, but rarely creates satisfaction.
apply: Check whether hygiene is fixed first (competitive pay, decent conditions)
Then recommend motivators – recognition, responsibility, growth – not just more money
pitfalls: Saying pay motivates in Herzberg – compensation is a hygiene factor
example: Scotland office: “great boss”, regular contact, recognition, get-togethers → motivators work despite weak pay link.

name: Equity theory
origin: Adams (1963) – named in the National Office Supplies case questions
purpose: Is pay perceived as fair? People compare their outcome/input ratio with others'.

parts.label: Comparison
points: My outcomes/inputs vs a referent's outcomes/inputs

parts.label: Reaction to inequity
points: Reduce effort, ask for more, distort perceptions, change referent, leave

apply: Find the referents in the case (other offices, colleagues, competitors) and the perceived inequity – then predict the reaction
example: Administrators unofficially getting part of the pot; a rep saying the package trails competitors; the London administrator job-hunting.

name: Pay transparency
purpose: What should employees have a right to know about pay?

parts.label: Low
points: Pay is confidential; employees know little about how pay is determined

parts.label: Process transparency
points: How to progress through the range

apply: Place the case firm on the scale and recommend a level – process transparency is the minimum for clear PRP rules
example: Share of job postings with salary information has risen since 2020 in the UK, France, Netherlands and sharply in Italy (Indeed data).

name: The EU pay transparency directive
purpose: Issue for any manager: can we explain and justify why different people are paid differently?

parts.label: Before recruitment
points: Applicants receive the starting pay or range before employment
Employers cannot ask about salary history

parts.label: During employment
points: Employees can request their pay level + average pay by sex for comparable work
Criteria for pay and progression accessible and gender-neutral

parts.label: Organizational accountability
points: Gender pay-gap reporting for employers with 100+ employees
≥ 5 % unexplained gap in a category can trigger a joint pay assessment

apply: Check whether the case's pay practices (discretion, secret pots, no criteria) could be explained and justified under the directive

name: Types of rewards
purpose: Which reward levers exist beyond money?

parts.label: Compensation (financial)
points: Variable pay: individual PRP, team bonus, profit sharing, equity

apply: Classify every reward in the case; recommend a mix – financial for hygiene and direction, non-financial as motivators
